newsitem.title: USA: Dismal 10-yr note sale completes refunding debacle.
newsitem.headline: Dismal 10-yr note sale completes refunding debacle.

text.p: For the second straight day, investors treated U.S. Treasury supply the way people treat a neighbor with a contagious disease: they stayed away in droves.

Demand for both Tuesday's three-year note and Wednesday's 10-year note sale, in which a combined $29 billion were sold, was virtually non-existent, which left dealers to take down the supply by themselves.

In the latest debacle, the Treasury sold $12 billion 10-year notes at an average 6.74 percent, a bit above market expectations. The bid-to-cover ratio at 1.86 was well below its recent average of 2.41 -- its lowest in two years and second lowest in seven years. Non-competitive bids were a paltry $383 million.
But the clincher was a nearly two-basis-point tail, after more than a one basis-point tail seen on the three-year auction.

"We had a hard time drumming up interest," said Tom Macirowski, senior Treasury market analyst at Goldman, Sachs & Co Inc. "The bullish camp didn't want to add more (securities), while the bearish camp was all flushed out.
"In that environment, we needed concessions," he added.
Yet the market did build in concessions, albeit not enough, players said.
When details of the auction were announced last week, the when-issued 10-year note was at 6.72 percent, only to fall to 6.67 late Tuesday.

"That underscores how bad the auction was," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and a money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. "We backed up seven basis points and still didn't see any demand."
The rout followed an equally disappointing three-year note auction on Tuesday.

"It is not a surprise. Market levels are a total contrast to fundamentals," said Chris Fitzmaurice, a 10-year trader at Salomon Bros. "And when you have joint intervention against the dollar, you are not going to see foreign participation."

Market participants said the main reason for the auctions' problems were because the market rallied way too much the past week, when Treasury yields fell to levels not seen since before the Federal Reserve tightened credit in late March. Some said the rally went too far too fast, creating an overbought situation.
"It's tough to get buyers at these levels," Flanagan said. "Just about everything was factored in short of a major slowing (of the economy) and that is not going to happen.
"We have the lowest unemployment rate in 23 years and the market rallies," he added. "That's going to catch up to you."
Many analysts said they believe the weakness seen in some of the recent data may be a reflection of strikes in the auto industry and flooding in the midwest.

"But there was enough uncertainty (of a rate hike) on May 20 leading people to be cautious," said Macirowski. He added that Goldman had little interest in the sale and that his salespeople remarked how other dealers didn't want the 10-year paper either.

The double-whammy of Treasury supply this week pushed bond yields significantly higher. Late Wednesday, the 30-year bond was at 6.96 percent, up from 6.88 on Monday, while the outstanding 10-year note was up to 6.76 percent from 6.65 percent.
But players lamented that the worst could be yet to come.
"Now we have to go through the motions distributing this paper," said Flanagan.
